paper.title: What Drives Representation Steering? A Mechanistic Case Study on Steering Refusal

read: full text: Sections 1-8, Limitations; Appendices B (vector curation, ASR evaluation), C (additional model results), D (metric comparisons) skimmed; A (derivation), E-H (EAP-IG, sparsity raw results, graphs, logit lens) skimmed

claims.claim: When a refusal steering vector is added at one layer of an instruction-tuned language model throughout multi-token generation, its effect on what the model writes is carried by a small part of the downstream network, and steering vectors for refusal obtained by quite different methods at that layer rely on essentially the same part. Supported only if, in each of three model families, a subgraph containing no more than about an eighth of the edges downstream of the steering layer recovers at least 85% of the steering effect on the generated tokens while the rest of the network recovers almost none; and if, for vectors made by at least three different methods, their subgraphs overlap by around 90% or more and each vector's effect is still mostly recovered (at least 85%) when routed through another method's subgraph, whereas a random subgraph twice the size recovers under 10%.
claims.decision_rule: Faithfulness >= 0.85 at <= ~12% of edges in 3 models, complement ~0; cross-method circuit overlap ~>=90% and interchanged circuits >= 0.85 faithful; random 2x circuit < 0.10.

claims.claim: A refusal steering vector changes a language model's behaviour through what attention heads write (their value and output pathway), and hardly at all through where attention heads look. Supported only if, across three model families and on both harmful prompts (where steering removes refusal) and harmless prompts (where it induces refusal), holding every layer's attention pattern fixed at its unsteered values changes the steered attack-success rate by less than 15% on average, while holding the value pathway fixed, removing only the vector's direct contribution to value inputs, or removing its direct contribution to MLP inputs each changes it by more than 40% on average; and if almost none of the most important downstream connections feed attention queries or keys.
claims.decision_rule: Freezing QK changes ASR <15% avg; freezing OV, removing direct value-input term, removing MLP direct term each >40% avg; top edges nearly never into Q/K.

claims.claim: Most dimensions of a refusal steering vector can be dropped without losing its effect if the kept dimensions are chosen by their measured causal contribution to the steered behaviour, and steering vectors made by different methods converge on a shared small subset of dimensions. Supported only if, in each of three models, zeroing at least 85% of the vector's dimensions chosen this way leaves most of its attack success intact on the evaluation sets, including a jailbreak benchmark never used to build or select the vector, and does so better at high sparsity than dropping dimensions at random or by smallest magnitude; and if the kept dimension sets of different methods' vectors overlap more than chance at every sparsity level (p < 0.05).
claims.decision_rule: >=85% sparsity retains most ASR in all three models incl. unseen benchmark; beats random dropout and bottom-k at >80% sparsity; cross-method IoU significant at every threshold.

experiments.text: Build and score the refusal steering vectors. Setup: harmful instructions from AdvBench, MaliciousInstruct, TDC2023 and HarmBench and harmless ones from Alpaca, 128 training and 32 validation each; test on 100 JailbreakBench harmful prompts and 100 held-out Alpaca prompts. Models: Gemma 2 2B Instruct, Llama 3.2 3B Instruct, Qwen 3 8B in non-thinking mode. Take the difference of mean activations between harmful and harmless prompts at each post-instruction position and layer, and keep the candidate that bypasses refusal on harmful validation prompts, induces it on harmless ones, and shifts harmless outputs by KL < 0.1 (chosen: layer 15 position -1, layer 12 position -4, layer 20 position -8). Add the vector at every position including the prompt, subtracting it to jailbreak and adding it to induce refusal. Score attack success on harmful prompts with the LlamaGuard 2 judge and on harmless prompts by refusal-substring matching. Result: steered attack success on JailbreakBench of 0.80, 0.85 and 0.83, and almost no compliance left on harmless prompts (0.00-0.03).

Adapt circuit discovery to steered multi-token generation. Setup: for each test prompt, generate greedy responses with and without steering and keep only pairs where steering flips the outcome. Treat the steered and unsteered hidden states as the clean and corrupted runs (and the reverse), teacher-force the response, and score each edge downstream of the steering layer by edge attribution patching with integrated gradients (10 steps) on the logit difference between steered and unsteered next tokens, averaged over response positions and masking positions where the two runs agree. Build circuits greedily from the scores and measure faithfulness as the share of the steering effect recovered when every edge outside the circuit is set to its unsteered activation.

Find how much of the network carries the steering effect. Setup: faithfulness of circuits of increasing size on JailbreakBench and Alpaca for the difference-of-means vector in all three models, with a circuit counted faithful at 0.85, plus faithfulness of each circuit's complement. Result: about 10% of Gemma's downstream edges (900 of 8,790), 11% of Llama's (13,500 of 124,441) and 8% of Qwen's (16,100 of 195,865) reach 0.85 average faithfulness, while the complements stay near 0 at every size.

Test whether vectors made by other methods use the same circuit. Setup: on Gemma and Llama, learn two more refusal vectors at the same layer, one by next-token prediction on prompt-response pairs that express refusal and one by preference optimisation on contrastive responses (pairwise cosine with the others only 0.10-0.42). Find each one's circuits, measure overlap |A and B| / min(|A|, |B|) across circuit sizes, and compute each vector's faithfulness when routed through every other vector's minimum faithful circuit, against a random circuit twice the minimum size. Result: all three need similar circuit sizes (preference optimisation slightly larger); overlap between any smaller and larger circuit is about 90% or more (0.84-1.00 Gemma, 0.77-0.98 Llama); interchanged circuits recover faithfulness strongly, while random circuits recover under 10%.

See which kind of component the important edges feed. Setup: take the top 100, 1,000 and 1,500 edges of the minimum faithful circuits for Gemma, Llama and Qwen and count incoming edges by downstream node type: MLP, attention query, key or value, and LM head. Result: in all three models almost no top edges enter attention queries or keys; they go to attention values, MLPs and the LM head.

Ablate each route by which the vector could act. Setup: with the difference-of-means vector in all three models, (a) freeze attention patterns by caching unsteered attention weights at each decoding step and patching them into the steered pass at every layer; (b) freeze attention values the same way; (c) subtract the normalised vector from every head's value-projection input, removing only its direct effect on values; (d) subtract it from every MLP input. Measure attack success on Alpaca and JailbreakBench. Result: freezing attention patterns changes it by only 8.83% on average (JailbreakBench 0.80 to 0.74 Gemma, 0.85 to 0.70 Llama, 0.83 to 0.70 Qwen), against 64.00% for freezing values (Llama Alpaca 0.03 to 0.99), 47.00% for removing the direct value term and 45.17% for removing the MLP term. The direct value term accounts for 73.4% of the drop from freezing values.

Read what the vector writes through each head. Setup: decompose each head's steered output into an input-independent term, the steering vector passed through the head's normalisation and value-output weights, and project it, the raw vector and the sum over heads onto the vocabulary with the logit lens, for all three vector types. Result: important heads surface refusal and harm words, e.g. Gemma layer 16 head 1 gives forbid, forbidding, prohibition for all three methods, and the sum over heads gives unethical, illegal, dangerous, even when the raw vector itself is not interpretable (Gemma's next-token vector, Llama's difference-of-means vector). One head with a large negative effect shows harmful words only after its sign is flipped, so it removes the concept during steering.

Sparsify the vector by measured contribution and compare with naive pruning. Setup: from the attribution scores, compute each dimension's normalised (gradient-based) and unnormalised (effect-based) contribution and zero dimensions below thresholds from 0 to 2.5; match the number of dropped dimensions with two baselines, dropping the smallest-magnitude dimensions and dropping at random. Average attack success over the three vector types on Alpaca (200 prompts), JailbreakBench and StrongReject, which was never used. Result: both attribution-based methods keep most attack success up to about 85% sparsity on Gemma, 96% on Llama and 88% on Qwen; keeping 9 of 3,072 Llama dimensions (99.7% sparse) lowers StrongReject success by only about 5%. Random dropout holds up to about 40% sparsity and smallest-magnitude pruning to about 80%, beyond which they fall well below the attribution-based methods.

Test whether different methods keep the same dimensions. Setup: at each sparsity threshold compute intersection over union of the non-zero dimensions of the three methods' sparsified vectors, against chance, with a hypergeometric test. Result: overlap stays above chance at all sparsities on Gemma and Llama, significant for every pair at every threshold above 0 (p < 0.05) and at p of about 1e-10 or below between 20% and 95% sparsity.

dropped: Metric and dataset-permutation robustness of the circuit framework (Appendix D; read only in outline, no numbers recorded); perplexity of sparsified steering; graph visualisations.
notes: c1 bar: 15% threshold covers the 8.83% average QK effect; per-model QK changes reach 15% on Llama JBB.
